findings.consequence: A request with optimized_pagination=true and a cursor with a negative offset returns a 500 error. The new path adds no working negative-offset capability. It only adds a crashable branch on a client-controlled value.
findings.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, get_result runs queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. Django querysets do not support negative indexing or slicing, and raise an assertion or ValueError. The comment claiming the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong. The endpoint sets enable_advanced_features=True for any admin who passes optimized_pagination=true. The cursor, including its offset, comes from the request's cursor parameter. A cursor with a negative offset, such as 0:-5:0, therefore raises an unhandled exception and a 500 instead of a page of results. If a negative start were accepted, stop = start + limit + extra could also become zero or negative, which would give inconsistent bounds.
findings.title: Negative cursor offset is sliced directly on the queryset, which Django rejects

prs.title: Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs

findings.consequence: A superuser or global-access member who sends a cursor with a negative offset together with optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 error from the audit log endpoint. The new 'advanced' path cannot return data. If the slice were somehow honored, it would let clients reach rows outside normal pagination bounds.
findings.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is true and the cursor offset is negative, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result runs queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset = cursor.offset. Django querysets reject negative indices with 'Negative indexing is not supported', so the comment saying the ORM handles negative slicing is wrong. The audit log endpoint turns the paginator on from the client-controlled `optimized_pagination=true` parameter, and the cursor offset also comes from the client. A cursor such as `0:-5:0` therefore raises an unhandled exception. A value like -1 with a small limit can also give a negative or zero stop. This is not a bounded optimization, because Django cannot execute a negative slice at all.
findings.title: Negative cursor offset is passed to Django queryset slicing, which raises instead of paginating

findings.consequence: Oversized segments are truncated without a metric or log, and the max_segment_spans setting is dead. Traces with parent chains deeper than 1000 may be split into separate segments.
findings.explanation: The Python check against self.max_segment_spans (default 1001) was removed from _load_segment_data. A hardcoded `span_count > 1000` trim in add-buffer.lua now replaces it. The max_segment_spans constructor argument is still accepted and stored but nothing reads it any more, so changing it has no effect. The trim also silently drops the lowest-timestamp spans with zpopmin instead of skipping the segment and logging an error. Separately, the redirect-chain loop bound went from 10000 to 1000. A span chain deeper than 1000 stops resolving, so the span lands in an intermediate set instead of the true root's set.
findings.title: Hardcoded 1000-span cap in Lua replaces configurable max_segment_spans, and the redirect limit drops from 10000 to 1000

After an operator changes `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, queries on the affected projects keep the old decision until the cache entry expires. This contradicts the comment in _are_all_projects_error_upsampled that the allowlist is read fresh each time to get the latest configuration.

findings.consequence: A user re-installing on an organization that has an Integration row with no sender metadata gets an unhandled 500 and cannot complete the install. The failure surfaces as a server error, not the intended 'could not verify' page.
findings.explanation: The new check in GitHubInstallation.dispatch reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. This path runs when an Integration row exists for the installation_id but has no OrganizationIntegration. Integrations created before this change, or created without a sender, have no `metadata["sender"]`. The sender is only copied into metadata conditionally in build_integration (around line 377). I did not check whether older rows lack the key. For such a row the lookup raises KeyError, or TypeError if `sender` is None, instead of returning the `error()` page. findings.consequence: A regression in handling a missing GitHub installation would go undetected, because the test passes whatever the 404 handling does.
findings.explanation: The test never runs the init step, and its callback uses state "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05". That value differs from the pipeline signature used by the other tests ("9cae5e88..."). In the OAuth step, `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` returns `error(request, ...)`, whose short message is "Invalid installation request." The new assertion matches that message, so the test passes on the state mismatch. It never reaches GitHubInstallation or `build_integration`, where the 404 from `/app/installations/{id}` becomes "The GitHub installation could not be found." The old assertion on that message was removed.

findings.consequence: Reports that violate either spec are accepted and counted in metrics. The endpoint previously rejected reports without a timestamp. Impact is limited because the endpoint only increments a metric.
findings.explanation: The old dataclass required `timestamp`. The new serializer makes both `age` and `timestamp` optional. The mutual-exclusion validators test `self.initial_data.get(...)` for truthiness. A report with `{"age": 5, "timestamp": 0}` or `{"age": 0, "timestamp": 5}` passes, although both fields are present. A report with neither field also passes validation. This contradicts the stated "present vs absent" intent in the docstrings and comments.
findings.title: age/timestamp exclusivity check uses truthiness and does not require either field

findings.consequence: ErrorEvent.id can be wrong when some error nodes are missing. The id is not used in the log message, so the effect is small.
findings.explanation: nodestore.get_multi returns a dict keyed by node id. Missing nodes may be omitted from that dict, and the values are not guaranteed to follow the order of error_ids. In either case zip(error_ids, events.values()) pairs the wrong id with the data. I did not check the nodestore backend implementation to see whether it omits missing keys.
findings.title: zip of error_ids with get_multi values can misalign ids

findings.consequence: The log sent to Seer places all errors at the start of the timeline, so the summary misattributes when errors occurred relative to user actions.
findings.explanation: gen_request_data compares error_events[i]['timestamp'] with event.get('timestamp', 0) for each replay event. Error timestamps come from nodestore event data, where they are epoch seconds (about 1.7e9). Replay recording events (rrweb) use epoch milliseconds (about 1.7e12). The two values are in different units, so every error compares as earlier than every replay event. All errors are emitted before the first replay event's message, and the chronological interleaving the code promises never happens. I did not read the nodestore event schema or the replay event format, so the unit mismatch rests on my knowledge of both formats.
findings.title: Error timestamps (seconds) compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)

findings.consequence: With more than one page of segments, the same error messages are duplicated in each page's Seer request and in each summary.
findings.explanation: analyze_recording_segments is used as on_results for a paginated response and runs once per page. Each call passes the full error_events list to gen_request_data. Errors earlier than the page's first event are emitted at the start of every page. Errors later than the page's last event are emitted at the end of every page. In both cases the same errors are repeated across pages.
findings.title: All error events are re-emitted on every paginated page

findings.consequence: Events with very long attachment names get a distorted or overflowing attachments table where they used to get an ellipsis.
findings.explanation: The removed FlexCenter in eventAttachments.tsx applied `overflowEllipsis` (overflow hidden, text-overflow ellipsis) and display:flex. The replacement `<Flex align="center">` has only flex and alignment. The grid column is `1fr` (minmax(auto,1fr)). The wrapper no longer has overflow hidden, so it no longer has a zero minimum size. Its min-content size now includes the full non-wrapping text of the inner `Name`. A long attachment file name therefore widens the first column instead of being truncated, which pushes the Size and Actions columns out of the table. The same wrapper change affects the `Flex` containers in the other edited files only in minor ways. For example, traceWaterfall also drops the old `height: 100%`.

findings.consequence: When the trace-items/attributes request fails, consumers see a loading state for several seconds, and the endpoint gets about four requests instead of one.
findings.explanation: The old hook called useApiQuery with retry: false. The new hook calls the raw useQuery with only enabled, queryKey and queryFn. DEFAULT_QUERY_CLIENT_CONFIG sets only refetchOnReconnect and refetchOnWindowFocus, so react-query's default of 3 retries with exponential backoff now applies. If the attributes endpoint returns an error, useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys throws, the query retries, and isFetching (exposed as isLoading) stays true until the retries finish. During that time attributes is the previous value, and error is not set until the last retry fails.
findings.title: Attribute-keys query now retries failures by default, keeping isLoading true

findings.consequence: In the default view, with no search text, the attributes that were meant to be hidden still appear in the span attributes table. They disappear as soon as the user types a query, so the table's contents depend on whether the search box is empty.
findings.explanation: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES is applied only inside the `.filter` that runs after the `if (!searchQuery.trim()) return sorted;` early return. With an empty search query, `sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns every attribute, so `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are shown. They are hidden only once the user types something. HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES is not referenced anywhere else in the eapSections directory, so nothing else removes them.
findings.title: Hidden attributes are only filtered out when a search query is entered

findings.consequence: A hung flusher is not killed on restart. Two flushers then run on the same shards, each with its own Kafka producer, and can produce duplicate segments. Each hang leaks a process, and `join` can leave child processes running on shutdown.
findings.explanation: The processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` derives from `BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`, a sibling class). So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False for every real process. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. In `_ensure_processes_alive` the kill is therefore skipped. When the cause is "hang", the stuck process stays alive and a new one is started for the same shards. The same check in `join` (line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either.
findings.title: Hung flusher process is never killed: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process fails for SpawnProcess

findings.consequence: On shutdown with a timeout, some flusher processes can be left running and not terminated. They are only cleaned up by daemon-exit handling, so they may keep flushing or producing during or after the consumer's shutdown.
findings.explanation: The old join() always called terminate() on the single flusher process after waiting. The new per-process loop does `break` when the shared deadline has passed. Any process that comes after that point never gets terminate() called. Example: with timeout=5 and three flusher processes, the first process's wait uses up the 5 seconds. The second and third are skipped and keep running.
findings.title: join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes once the deadline expires

findings.consequence: The test does not wait for the flusher to process the drift change. The assertion `(msg,) = messages` still depends on a race between the flusher and `step.join()`, so the test can fail intermittently. The added sleep gives no protection.
findings.explanation: test_basic starts with monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None). That replaces the attribute on the time module for the whole test. The added `time.sleep(0.1)` runs after the drift change and looks up `time.sleep` at call time, so it calls the patched lambda and returns at once. The comment says "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", but no wait happens. The same patch is why the sleep in `test_flusher_processes_limit` never waits either.
findings.title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because the test patches time.sleep

findings.consequence: The `queued` value is stale for every assignment source. It grows more wrong the longer the worker or web process runs. Anything that reads `queued` for ordering, staleness or cycle detection will get wrong results.
findings.explanation: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass default, so `timezone.now()` runs once when the module is imported. Every `AssignmentSource` built through `from_integration` gets that same fixed timestamp, which is the process start time, not the time the assignment was queued. `to_dict` then sends this wrong value to the task through `asdict`. The fix is `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. This also stops the datetime from being frozen into the class definition.
findings.title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time

findings.consequence: Once an offset gap occurs, the partition's committed offset freezes. After a restart or rebalance, all messages past the gap are reprocessed. all_offsets also leaks memory for the lifetime of the consumer.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets walks range(start, max_offset+1) and breaks at the first offset that is not in all_offsets. It treats a missing offset as unprocessed. Kafka offsets are not always contiguous, for example with transaction control records or compacted topics. Suppose offsets 5 and 7 are submitted and 6 never reaches the consumer. Commit then stops at 5. After mark_committed(5), start is 6 and offset 6 is not in all_offsets, so the loop breaks immediately on every later call. Nothing above 5 on that partition is ever committed again. The tracker never skips a gap, and all_offsets grows without bound.
findings.title: Offset gap permanently stalls commits for a partition

findings.consequence: After any rebalance, thread-queue-parallel mode silently skips processing every message while still committing its offsets, so check-in results are lost permanently.
findings.explanation: The factory builds one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and hands the same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker. create_with_partitions runs again on every partition rebalance. The strategy's close(), terminate() and join() call queue_pool.shutdown() (queue_consumer.py:335-345). That sets worker.shutdown, shuts down the queues and joins the workers, so the shared pool is dead after the first rebalance. The factory never recreates the pool: it only sets queue_pool to None in its own shutdown(). The next strategy therefore gets a pool with no live workers. Each queue.put in FixedQueuePool.submit raises ShutDown. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches it and marks the offset added and completed without processing it. The offset tracker (including last_committed) is also shared across assignments and carries stale state.
findings.title: Shared queue pool is shut down by strategy close() and reused after rebalance, dropping messages

findings.consequence: A regression that serializes subscriptions across workers would not be caught.
findings.explanation: `test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions` says it verifies that different subscriptions are processed concurrently. It only asserts `call_count == 2`, which a serial implementation also satisfies. The processor mock has no barrier or overlap check.
findings.title: Concurrency test does not check concurrency

findings.consequence: The test cannot verify that a processing error leaves later offsets committable. A regression where a failed message blocks commits would go undetected, and the assertion actively encodes the wrong expectation.
findings.explanation: The test docstring says errors must not block offset commits. The implementation completes the offset in a `finally` in OrderedQueueWorker.run (queue_consumer.py:148-149), so a failed offset 100 and a successful offset 101 are both committable, and the commit loop would commit {partition: 102}. The test asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which is the opposite of that behavior. It passes only because the commit loop first fires after a 1s wait (queue_consumer.py:276) and the test checks about 0.3s after processing finishes. It can never detect the behavior it names. It would fail, or be flaky, if the commit thread ran sooner.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting its docstring and the implementation; passes only by timing

findings.consequence: Processing any metric_alert_fire detector crashes process_detectors with TypeError. Before the change, the handler was instantiable and returned an empty list. It also aborts processing of the remaining detectors in the same call.

findings.consequence: Organizers can confirm pending bookings that are unpaid but have the payment app enabled. The old code blocked this.
findings.explanation: The old condition was `(isPending && !paymentAppData.enabled) || (paymentAppData.enabled && !!price && booking.paid)`. It is now `(isPending && !showPendingPayment) || (showPendingPayment && booking.paid)`, where `showPendingPayment = enabled && payment.length && !paid`. The second clause can never be true, because showPendingPayment requires !paid. A pending booking with the payment app enabled, no payment rows and paid=false makes showPendingPayment falsy, so Confirm is shown. The old code hid Confirm in that case.

findings.consequence: Users can no longer use "check for recordings" on past Cal Video bookings that have no recording yet. Recordings that exist but are not yet marked isRecorded cannot be fetched from the booking list.
findings.explanation: The old code enabled the recordings button for past, confirmed Cal Video bookings that were not yet recorded. It labelled the button "check_for_recordings" so the user could fetch recordings. The refactor adds `(action.id === "view_recordings" && !booking.isRecorded)` to `disabled` in BookingListItem. getVideoOptionsActions in bookingActions.ts also sets `disabled: !(... && booking.isRecorded)` and uses the plain "view_recordings" label. For a past, confirmed Cal Video booking with isRecorded=false, the action is now always disabled, so the dialog that checks for recordings can never be opened. The old behavior of showing recordings for any recorded booking regardless of location is also changed: with isCalVideoLocation now required, recorded bookings at other locations are disabled.

findings.consequence: After a successful save, or any refetch that returns changed data, the event type editor unmounts and remounts. In-progress form state is lost, the UI flickers, and extra refetches are triggered.
findings.explanation: The effect cleanup invalidates and resets the event-type query. This cleanup was meant to run only on unmount or when the id changed. The change adds `eventTypeQueryData` to the dependency array, so the cleanup now also runs every time the cached data changes. Examples are a refetch that returns different data after a save invalidates the query, or a window-focus refetch. When that happens, the cleanup from the previous render closes over truthy data and calls `resetQueries`. That clears the data, so `if (!eventTypeQueryData) return null` unmounts the whole EventType form. The form then remounts after a refetch.
findings.title: Adding eventTypeQueryData to effect deps resets the query and unmounts the form whenever data changes

findings.consequence: Any CommonJS consumer that calls require("@calcom/atoms") fails with a module-not-found error. Tools that resolve "main" also fail. Before the change these consumers failed differently or fell through to the ESM entry. Now the package.json points at a missing file.
findings.explanation: The change adds "require": "./dist/cal-atoms.umd.cjs" to the "." export and sets "main" to "./dist/cal-atoms.umd.cjs". vite.config.ts builds the lib with formats: ["es"] and rollupOptions.output.format "esm". Only dist/cal-atoms.js is emitted, so the .umd.cjs file does not exist. The config sets no UMD or CJS output anywhere, so nothing else generates it.

findings.consequence: Routing form analytics and filters show the wrong host's name, email and avatar after a booking is reassigned. The wrong data persists until the response itself is updated.
findings.explanation: booking_update_trigger_for_routing_form fires on UPDATE OF "userId" (among other columns). The trigger function trigger_refresh_routing_form_response_denormalized_booking sets "bookingUserId" = NEW."userId", but it does not update "bookingUserName", "bookingUserEmail" or "bookingUserAvatarUrl". The user-update trigger only fires on changes to the users row, so nothing else refreshes these columns. Example: a booking is reassigned from user A to user B. The denormalized row then has bookingUserId = B but still has A's name, email and avatar.

findings.consequence: If getCalendar or the calendar deleteEvent call fails during a reschedule, the error is not logged by the intended handler. It surfaces as an unhandled rejection, which can crash the process or be silently lost. Calendar events can also be left undeleted while the reschedule flow reports success.
findings.explanation: The change turned the forEach callback into an async function that awaits getCalendar. This happens in vital/lib/reschedule.ts and wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts, both at lines 125-135, and the same pattern is in bookings.tsx at lines 553-566. Before the change, a synchronous throw from getCalendar, such as a CalendarService constructor error, was caught by the try/catch around the forEach. Now the throw, and any rejection from deleteEvent, happens inside an un-awaited promise. The try/catch never sees it, and the error becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Because the loop no longer waits for the deletions, the code after it (sending emails and webhooks) runs before the calendar events are deleted.
findings.title: async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective

findings.explanation: TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable is now `disable(password: string, code: string, backupCode: string)`. The change updated apps/web/components/settings/DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx, but apps/web/components/security/DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx:38 still calls `TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable(password, totpCode)`. That call no longer satisfies the signature, so TypeScript reports "Expected 3 arguments, but got 2".

findings.consequence: An unauthenticated attacker who knows only an email address can sign in as any user without 2FA enabled, including admins in dev. For 2FA users, the password factor is bypassed.
findings.explanation: The identity-provider checks and the password check in authorize (lines 113-129) all depend on `!credentials.totpCode`. A request with a victim's email and any non-empty totpCode, with no password, skips all three. If the user has twoFactorEnabled=false, neither the backup-code branch (line 131) nor the TOTP branch (line 157) runs. Nothing later verifies the password or rejects a totpCode when 2FA is off. Line 205 then returns the user object, which means the sign-in succeeds. The same holds for users with a non-CAL identity provider. If 2FA is enabled, the password is still skipped, so a valid TOTP alone is enough to log in. The backup-code branch added by this change has the same problem: totpCode plus backupCode skips the password check.
findings.title: Password check skipped whenever totpCode is supplied; authorize returns user with no credential verified

findings.consequence: A single-use 2FA backup code can be replayed in parallel requests. The impact is limited because the attacker must already know the password and a valid code.
findings.explanation: In authorize, the encrypted backupCodes blob is read in the earlier findUnique. It is decrypted and checked with indexOf. The matching slot is then nulled and the whole blob is written back with prisma.user.update, keyed only on id. There is no transaction and no compare-and-swap on the stored blob. Two concurrent logins with the same valid code and password both read the blob before either write lands. Both pass indexOf and both succeed. The concurrent writes can also overwrite each other, so a second code used in parallel can be restored. Login guessing is rate-limited: checkRateLimitAndThrowError runs on each authorize call with the user's email. disable.ts has no limiter, but it requires an authenticated session and the password for CAL users.
findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so a single-use code can be accepted twice

prs.title: feat: 2fa backup codes

findings.consequence: Without an explicit externalCalendarId, `deleteEvent` falls back to the "primary" calendar instead of the booking's destination calendar. The event is not found there, or the wrong calendar is touched, so the event is not deleted. In `updateEvent`, `calendarId` becomes undefined and the Google API call fails or targets the wrong calendar.
findings.explanation: In `deleteEvent` (line 317) and `updateEvent` (line 256), the fallback runs only when `externalCalendarId` is falsy. It then calls `destinationCalendar.find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)`. That compares each calendar's externalId to the same falsy value, so it only matches an entry with a null, undefined or empty externalId, and the result is undefined. The old code used `destinationCalendar.externalId`. The change should have used the first destination calendar, as the other services do with `[mainHostDestinationCalendar]`.
findings.title: Google Calendar update/delete fallback to destinationCalendar can never match

findings.consequence: Creating an event with Google Meet as the location for a host with no destination calendar crashes instead of falling back to Cal Video. This breaks the booking or confirmation flow.
findings.explanation: `destinationCalendar` is now an array, and the changed callers (bookingReminder, confirm.handler, editLocation.handler) pass `[]` when there is no destination calendar. `create` destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];`, so the variable is `undefined` for an empty or missing array. It then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was safe. When `evt.location === MeetLocationType` and no destination calendar exists, the `.integration` access throws `Cannot read properties of undefined`. The intended fallback to `integrations:daily` never runs.
findings.title: EventManager.create throws TypeError for Google Meet location when destinationCalendar is empty

findings.consequence: The collected team members' calendars never reach evt. EventManager and the booking's destinationCalendar connect only see an empty or null list, so no calendar event is created for those hosts.
findings.explanation: evt.destinationCalendar is set to null when the event type and the organizer have no destination calendar. The later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` does nothing on null. Take a COLLECTIVE event where the organizer (first user) has no destinationCalendar and another host has one. That host's calendar is collected into teamDestinationCalendars, then silently discarded.

findings.consequence: On self-hosted instances without team billing, every organization is created with no slug, so its URL and routing are broken. On billing-enabled instances, the slug is claimed before payment and the pending-slug flow is bypassed.
findings.explanation: The old code set `slug` on the organization only when `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED`. When billing is enabled, the slug was left out and kept only as `requestedSlug` in metadata until payment. The new code is `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, which drops the negation. Both `startTime` and `endTime` are minutes in the organizer's timezone, but they are compared against UTC hour and minute and the UTC weekday of the slot. findings.consequence: After the first successful token refresh, every Google Calendar credential is overwritten with a malformed key. Later parses of that key throw, so the integration breaks for those users until they reconnect.

The Office365 caller has the same pattern in a milder form: it checks `.success` on a result that now throws on failure, so the `.success &&` guard is dead code and failures now throw instead of being handled.

findings.consequence: Permanently unschedulable SMS reminders are re-evaluated on every cron run until their scheduledDate passes. findings.consequence: With overlapping cron invocations, failing reminders can take more retries than intended to pass the `retryCount > 1` cleanup threshold. Duplicate SMS can also be scheduled for the same reminder. Both effects are limited to cron overlap.

Both updates are keyed only on `id`, with no `scheduled: false` condition. If two cron runs overlap, both read the same retryCount and both write N+1, so one failure is lost. Both runs also pick up the same unscheduled reminder, so both can call twilio.scheduleSMS for it. Each run then sets scheduled=true with its own sid, so the user gets a duplicate SMS. With both on the classpath, the sort in detectProvider (CryptoIntegration.java, the new .sorted(...) line) has a tie. Collectors/sorted is stable, so the winner is whichever one ServiceLoader returns first, which depends on classpath order. The old code failed fast in this case. The new code silently picks one and logs the other only at debug level. The Elytron provider returns null from getBouncyCastleProvider and the default one uses BouncyCastle, so the two behave differently. Classpath ordering can therefore change which crypto implementation handles keys, signatures and certificates, with no error or warning.

findings.consequence: The regression test for concurrent group deletion and reading can pass while the race it targets still occurs, and it can leave a runaway thread if a delete fails.
findings.explanation: createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a background thread that loops on groups().groups(...). The test then sets deletedAll to true and immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty. It never joins the thread. A read that is in flight when the flag flips can still throw after the assertion has run. That is likely here, because the last deletions are the ones most likely to race with the read. The exception goes into the list after it was checked, so the test passes. The thread is also non-daemon and is not stopped in a finally block. If a delete throws, deletedAll is never set and the loop runs forever.
findings.title: Concurrent reader thread is never joined, so the test can miss failures

findings.consequence: Following the unsubscribe link from an email twice, or having a link scanner fetch it, silently mutes the topic for the user. A user with no TopicUser record gets a server error instead of the unsubscribe page.
findings.explanation: `TopicsController#unsubscribe` is routed as a GET (`t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe`). It changes state on every request: a level above regular becomes regular, and anything else becomes muted. A second load of the same URL, such as a refresh, a back/forward navigation, or an email client link prefetcher, therefore moves a user from regular to muted. Separately, `TopicUser.find_by(...)` can return nil for a user who has no TopicUser row for the topic, for example one notified by a mention. In that case `tu.notification_level` raises NoMethodError and the user gets a 500.
findings.title: Unsubscribe GET toggles notification level and crashes when no TopicUser row exists

findings.consequence: The match_count statistic is inaccurate under concurrent or repeated validation. Each lookup also costs an extra UPDATE with its own uniqueness query. The impact is limited because blocking itself still works.
findings.explanation: should_block? is called from EmailValidator#validate_each, so it runs on every validation of a User whose email changed. It loads the record, increments match_count in Ruby, and saves it. Two concurrent signups with the same blocked email both read the same count, and one increment is lost. Each extra validation pass (for example valid? followed by save) also counts as another match, and the lookup is an exact, case-sensitive match. A write that can overwrite a concurrent one therefore happens inside a validator, which should be side-effect free.
findings.title: should_block? updates match_count with a non-atomic read-modify-write inside a validation

findings.consequence: Admins see a spurious empty page and an enabled "next" button for any group whose member count is a non-zero multiple of the page size (50, 100, and so on).
findings.explanation: In admin-group.js.es6, `totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. For a group with exactly 50 members and limit 50, this gives 2 pages instead of 1. `showingLast` compares `currentPage` with `totalPages`, so on page 1 it is false and `next` is allowed. `next` then sets offset = min(0+50, 50) = 50. `findMembers` requests offset 50 and gets an empty member list, so the admin lands on a blank page 2.
findings.title: totalPages overcounts by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit

findings.consequence: Admins see a phantom empty last page in the group member list, and the group members page shares the same model. The off-by-one lives in the new pagination logic (group.js offset clamp together with the totalPages formula in admin-group.js.es6).
findings.explanation: findMembers clamps the offset to user_count, not to the last valid page start. The admin-group controller computes totalPages as floor(user_count/limit)+1 and the group.js clamp uses the same boundary. With 50 members and limit 50, totalPages is 2, so "next" is enabled on page 1. Next sets offset = min(0+50, 50) = 50, and the server then returns an empty members list for offset 50. The UI shows page 2/2 with no members. The same happens for any count that is an exact multiple of the limit.

findings.consequence: When embedding is on (`__rest_serializer === "1"`), a null `*_ids` field throws and the model fails to load. An unresolved id yields a `colors` array with undefined items, so later code that dereferences them will fail. The original `*_ids` data is also lost.
findings.explanation: In _hydrateEmbedded the new `*_ids` branch calls `obj[k].map(...)` with no guard. A payload with `color_ids: null` (or any non-array) throws a TypeError. That aborts hydration of the whole response, because the regex also matches any key ending in `_ids`. `_lookupSubType` returns undefined when the sub-collection is missing from the root or the id is not found. Those undefined values stay in the array, so `obj.colors` contains undefined entries. `hydrated || []` never applies, because an array is always truthy. The key is deleted and replaced unconditionally. The singular branch only rewrites the key when the lookup succeeds, so the two branches behave differently.
